Node B, the query, is outlined in the accent color with its id 2 highlighted. The card returns the Node object Node(id=2, label='B')." width="100%"} Retrieves the `Node` object for the specified node. The `Node` object has three properties: `id` (the integer node ID), `label` (the string label, or `None` if the node has no label), and `attributes` (a dict of the node's attributes, including `type` if one was set, or `None` if the node has no attributes). This is the quickest way to inspect everything stored on a single node, for example when debugging how a graph was built or reading a few attributes inside a loop. To look at many nodes at once, `get_node_df()` returns all of them as a table. A node that doesn't exist raises a `ValueError`, whether it was given as an ID or a label; use `has_node()` to test for existence. The `attributes` dict is a copy, so changing it doesn't change the graph; use `set_node_attrs()` for that. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [node]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Union[int, str]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The node to retrieve, given either as its integer node ID or as its string label. An `int` is always treated as an ID and a `str` always as a label, so `"2"` looks for a node labelled `"2"`, not the node with ID `2`. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Node]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The `Node` object. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `node=` is an ID or label that doesn't match any node. [TypeError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If `node=` is neither an `int` nor a `str`. ::: ## Examples {.doc-examples} `get_node()` accepts either a label or an internal ID, and returns the underlying `Node` object with its `id`, `label`, and `attributes`: ::: {#f1fc3d5b .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph().add_node(label="A", color="red", size=10).add_node(label="B") node = graph.get_node("A") node.id ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 1 ``` ::: ::: The label is tracked separately from the auto-assigned ID: ::: {#e7ecd41d .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} node.label ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` 'A' ``` ::: ::: Any extra keyword arguments passed to `add_node()` are stored in `attributes`: ::: {#3b7e81be .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} node.attributes ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` {'color': 'red', 'size': 10} ``` ::: ::: Passing an integer looks the node up by ID instead. Node `"B"` was added second, so it has ID `2`: ::: {#3ae9b7ba .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.get_node(2) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` Node(id=2, label='B') ``` ::: ::: An ID that isn't in the graph raises, so test with `has_node()` first when a node may be missing: ::: {#2f208919 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} graph.has_node(99) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` False ``` ::: :::
